draft.title: Fiscal policy
card: Fiscal policy is the government's use of its spending and taxes to influence the economy. The Australian Government sets it, usually through the federal Budget.
the government spends more, cuts taxes, or does both. It aims to lift spending and support jobs, so it may be used in a slowdown.
the government spends less, raises taxes, or does both. It aims to slow spending, so it may be used when the economy is growing too fast and prices are rising quickly.
Spending includes things like roads, hospitals and payments to households. Taxes take money out of household and business incomes, so changing them changes how much people can spend.
draft.remember: Fiscal policy changes government spending and taxes to push the economy up or slow it down.

a.q: Which of these is an example of fiscal policy?
opts: The government builds new hospitals to create jobs
A business hires more workers to meet demand
A family saves more of its income each month
A shop cuts prices to sell more of its stock
a.why: Building hospitals is government spending, and it can support jobs. The other three are choices made by businesses or households, not by the government, so they are not fiscal policy.
a.clue: Fiscal policy is about what the government spends and collects.

b.q: Wages are rising fast in Australia, spending is strong and prices are climbing quickly. Which fiscal policy response fits best?
opts: Raise taxes so households have less to spend
Cut taxes so households have more to spend
Fund extra projects to create more jobs
Pay more to households to lift their spending
b.why: Higher taxes leave households with less to spend, which can slow demand and ease price rises. Cutting taxes is tempting because it helps households, but it would add to spending when the economy is already running hot.
b.clue: The aim is to slow spending, not to boost it.

a.best: The government builds new hospitals to create jobs

b.best: Raise taxes so households have less to spend

problems.detail: The clue 'The aim is to slow spending, not to boost it' gives the answer away. Only one option slows spending, so students can pick it without reading the scenario as an overheating economy.
